name: PasswordHash
description: How a password is stored and verified. Both implementations must accept exactly the same passwords for the same rows, including rows written by legacy — so both schemes are specified here, not just the new one.
principle: The stored value records which scheme produced it. A global configuration setting cannot do that, which is why the legacy column has to be replaced rather than retuned.

schemes.description: Carried over so existing logins keep working. Reproduced here because the fast path must verify these rows too.
algorithm: salt_source = email (EMAIL) or gradido_id (GRADIDO_ID), per users.password_encryption_type
key = argon2id(password, salt = h[0..16], t = 10, m = 32 MiB, p = 1, output 32 bytes)
stored = SipHash-2-4(key, LOGIN_SERVER_KEY), 8 bytes, little endian, held as uint64
notes: SipHash-2-4 (libsodium crypto_shorthash) is documented as a hash-table primitive, not as collision resistant. The security of this scheme rests on LOGIN_SERVER_KEY staying secret rather than on the hash: without the key an attacker cannot even test a candidate.

64 bits is not the weak link here. A collision search costs about 2^63 argon2id evaluations; the password's own entropy gives out long before that. The reason to leave the scheme is agility, not width.
The salt derives from a public and, for EMAIL, mutable identifier. Changing the email invalidates the password — which is why PasswordEncryptionType exists at all.

schemes.status: current — write this for every new or changed password
algorithm: salt = 16 random bytes from the OS CSPRNG, per password, never derived from user data
hash = argon2id(peppered, salt, parameters from const.json, output 32 bytes)
stored = the encoded PHC string, parameters included
notes: Parameters live in the stored string, so they can be raised for new passwords without touching existing rows and without a coordinated rehash.
The pepper stays outside the database. A dumped table alone is not testable.
Verification parses the parameters out of the stored string and uses those, never the current defaults — otherwise every raise of the defaults locks out every existing user.

rules: Select the scheme from users.password_encryption_type. Never guess it from the column contents.
NO_PASSWORD (0) always fails verification. It is not an empty password and not a wildcard.
Compare in constant time. For the PHC scheme this is required; the comparison must not return early on the first differing byte.

On a successful verification against LEGACY_SHORTHASH, rehash the password with ARGON2ID_PHC and write both the new column and the new password_encryption_type in the same transaction. This is the only migration path — there is no offline conversion, because the plaintext exists only during a login.
A failed login reports one outcome to the client regardless of cause. The log may say which of unknown_contact, wrong_password, not_verified or deleted it was — see logging.json, auth.login.failed.
LOGIN_APP_SECRET must be present and of the expected length. A missing or short pepper aborts startup — it must never silently degrade to hashing without one.
LOGIN_SERVER_KEY must be present as long as any row still uses LEGACY_SHORTHASH.

neverLogged: the stored hash or PHC string

open.question: Which argon2id parameters for new hashes, against the memory budget of the fast path?
open.detail: Legacy uses 32 MiB x 10 passes, about half a second. That is 32 MiB per concurrent login attempt on an unauthenticated endpoint, against a fast server whose whole resident set is ~15 MB. Legacy's defence is a worker queue that answers 'Server is full' when saturated — which is itself the denial of service, just with a friendlier message.
open.decide: a concurrency cap for password verification, plus rate limiting per account and per address, before the parameters are fixed. Rate limiting is the actual defence; the queue is a symptom.
open.status: unanswered — the values in const.json are legacy's, carried over so nothing gets weaker by accident, not because they were chosen for gradido2
